profiled_workloads.selection_reason: Lowest eval speedup (0.2751x) and simultaneously the highest absolute latency (0.0910 ms) among the timing set; bfloat16 4096x4096, i.e. the single worst regime and the shape that dominates the geo_mean loss. Profiled at both metrics and instruction level.

Second-worst speedup (0.2854x) at 0.0886 ms; float32 4096x4096 is a distinct regime from the 16-bit cases (no widening needed for the compare, different UB budget, different tile count), so it must be represented separately rather than inferred from bf16.

Boundary workload of the large-shape regime: float16 4096x4096 at 0.4605x is the best of the three big cases while still far above the small-case floor, so it isolates whether the large-shape loss is dtype-independent or fp16-specific.

Cheapest possible control (float32, 1024 elements, 0.8330x): it sits on the host-launch floor where device work is negligible, so it separates launch-overhead cost from kernel cost and lets the large-case signal be attributed correctly. Also used to test whether the collection failure was workload-size dependent.

performance_interpretation:
No profiler measurement was obtained this round, so I make no claim about pipeline utilization, DMA granularity, vector-instruction mix, or synchronization for this snapshot. The following is explicit inference from (a) the authoritative eval comparison returned by get_profile_context and (b) the candidate source at .kernelgen/evals/round-0001/main.py (sha256 3a7da241...); it is hypothesis generation, not measured truth.

FACT (eval, this round): the nine <=1M-element timing cases are tightly clustered at 0.812-0.849x with latencies 0.0122-0.0133 ms against 0.0103-0.0109 ms references - a near-constant ~2.0-2.1 us additive penalty, consistent with a launch/dispatch floor rather than device work. The three 4096x4096 cases are categorically different: fp16 0.0500 ms (0.4605x), bf16 0.0910 ms (0.2751x), fp32 0.0886 ms (0.2854x). The 4096x4096 cases move 16x the data of the 1048576-element tier; since the small cases are already at the floor, essentially the entire geo_mean deficit (0.6582 vs the 0.8 target) is produced by these three cases. The bf16 and fp32 large cases take ~1.8x the fp16 large case while moving half the bytes, so whatever dominates scales inversely with element width (per-element instruction cost, not bytes).

INFERENCE: per-element vector-instruction count is the leading suspect. `_expm1_value` evaluates BOTH branches of a `tl.where` for every element (SIMT vectors have no short-circuit): `tl.abs`, a compare, the 2-term series `x * (1.0 + 0.5 * x)`, `tl.exp(x)`, `tl.exp(x) - 1.0`, and the select. In this Triton-Ascend build plain Python float constants are widened to fp32 (the candidate's own comments record `arith.extf f16 -> f32` for the compare against a scalar and for `tl.fma(x, 0.5, 1.0)`), so on the 16-bit paths the series and the `- 1.0` additionally carry extf/truncf traffic around an fp32 ALU sequence, and the select crosses widths. That predicts a vector workload several times the reference's native expm1 and a cost that grows as element width shrinks (more of the tile is spent on conversion bookkeeping per useful lane), which matches the bf16 > fp32 > fp16 ordering of the eval data. The tile geometry is already a per-dtype best-effort (fp16 8192x2, bf16 8192x1, fp32 4096x2), so remaining headroom is unlikely to be in tile size.

What this inference does NOT establish: whether `tl.exp` itself, the compare/select, or the type conversions dominate; whether the masked `tl.load(..., mask=, other=0.0)` lowers to one contiguous DMA per tile or is split; and whether the large-case time is serialized fetch->compute->writeback rather than overlapped. Those three questions are exactly what the failed msprof collection would have answered, and they remain OPEN.

next_experiment.action_description: Make `_expm1_value` branch-free: for all three dtypes return `tl.exp(x) - 1.0` computed in the input element type, and delete the `tl.where(tl.abs(x) < TINY, x * (1.0 + 0.5 * x), ...)` series selection together with its TINY tensor and the abs/compare. Change only that helper; keep the per-dtype tiles, the persistent-loop launch path, the masks and the wrapper untouched, so the measurement isolates the value function. The tolerance contract makes this numerically defensible without chasing the reference: the small-|x| error of `exp(x) - 1` is bounded by half an ulp of exp(x) ~ 1 (about 4.9e-4 for fp16/bf16, about 6e-8 for fp32), while the contract's constant term is atol=1.5e-2 for fp16/bf16 and 1e-4 for fp32. Before committing, verify this bound numerically against torch.expm1 on a dense sweep of |x| below the current thresholds at each dtype and confirm it stays inside atol + rtol*|reference|.
next_experiment.expected_impact: Removes roughly half the per-element vector operations (abs, compare, 3-op series, and the extf/truncf chain around them, plus one wide select) and leaves a single transcendental against a constant. Because the small cases are already pinned at the launch floor and only the three 4096x4096 cases carry the deficit, this can move geo_mean only through them: if the compare/series/conversion terms are a large share of vector time, expect the three big cases to move materially (fp16 0.46x / bf16 0.275x / fp32 0.285x trending toward 0.55-0.70x) and geo_mean toward or past 0.70. If vector time barely moves, `tl.exp` dominates, which is itself the decisive answer and redirects effort to overlap/pipelining.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: Accuracy risk concentrated at small |x|: relative error grows without bound as |x| shrinks, and only the absolute tolerance term absorbs it, so the full 18-case correctness suite must pass with matched_ratio 1.0 and a dense small-|x| sweep must be checked before adoption. Second risk is the sign of zero: expm1(-0.0) is -0.0 while exp(-0.0)-1.0 is +0.0; a compare-free version loses that sign, so if a correctness case or review flags negative zero, reinstate exactly one compare against zero plus a select (x==0 -> x) and re-measure - that still keeps the series and abs deleted. Third, the fp16/bf16 overflow boundary shifts by one ulp (exp(x) can overflow where expm1 does not); this band is already present in the current code for all |x| >= TINY, so it is not a new exposure, but confirm the special-value cases still pass. Rollback is a single-file revert to main.py sha256 3a7da241fbbbdf27981cdd098c9030ed9cbc4ccc3de19710a05254e47a4482f0; do not retune tiles in the same round, so the result stays attributable.
